text: Chapter 6: "There

Was Someone Crying—There Was!"

The next day, the rain poured down in torrents again. When Mary looke
d out of her window, the moor was almost completely hidden by gray mist and clouds. Going outside today was out of the question.

“What do you do in your cottage when it rains like this?” she asked Martha.

“We mostly just try to stay out of each other's way,”
Martha answered.

“Oh, it really feels like there are a lot of us then! Mother is a good-tempered woman, but she gets completely overwhelmed. The oldest ones go out to the cow shed and play there. Dickon doesn't mind the wet at all. He goes out just the same as if the sun were shining. He says he sees things on rainy days that don't show when the weather is nice. Once he found a little fox cub half-drowned in its hole, and he brought it home inside his shirt to keep it warm. Its mother had been killed nearby, the hole was flooded, and the rest of the litter was dead. He still has it at home now. Another time, he found a half-drowned young crow and brought it home too, and tamed it. He named it Soot because it's so black, and it hops and flies around with him everywhere.”

By this time, Mary had forgotten to resent Martha’s familiar way of talking. She had even begun to find it interesting, and she felt sorry when Martha stopped talking or went away. The stories her Ayah had told her in India were completely different from the ones Martha told about the moorland cottage. That cottage housed fourteen people who lived in four tiny rooms and never had quite enough to eat. The children seemed to tumble around and amuse themselves like a litter of energetic, good-natured collie puppies. Mary was drawn most of all to the mother and Dickon. Whenever Martha told stories about what her mother said or did, they always sounded warm and comforting.
“If I had a raven or a fox cub, I could play with it,”
Mary said.
“But I have nothing.”
Martha looked puzzled.
“Can you knit?”
she asked.
“No,”
Mary answered.
“Can you sew?”
“No.”
“Can you read?”
“Yes.”
“Then why don't you read something, or practice your spelling? You're old enough to be learning from books by now.”
“I don't have any books,”
Mary said.
“The ones I had were left in India.”
“That’s a pity,”
Martha said.
“If Mrs. Medlock would let you go into the library, there are thousands of books in there.”

Mary didn't ask where the library was, because she was suddenly struck by a new idea. She made up her mind to go and find it herself. She wasn't worried about Mrs. Medlock, who seemed to spend all her time in her comfortable housekeeper's sitting room downstairs. In this strange place, you hardly ever saw anyone. In fact, there was no one to see but the servants. When their master was away, they lived a comfortable life downstairs. There was a huge kitchen decorated with polished brass and pewter, and a large servants’ hall where they ate four or five hearty meals every day. A lot of lively fun went on there when Mrs. Medlock was out of the way.

Mary's meals were served regularly, and Martha waited on her, but nobody paid any attention to her. Mrs. Medlock came to check on her every day or two, but no one asked what she was doing or told her what to do. She figured this was probably the English way of raising children. In India, she had always been attended by her Ayah, who followed her everywhere and waited on her hand and foot. Mary had often grown tired of her company. Now, nobody followed her at all, and she was learning to dress herself because Martha looked at her as if she were silly and stupid whenever she wanted things handed to her and put on.
“Don't you have any common sense?”
Martha had said once, when Mary just stood there waiting for her to put on her gloves.
“Our Susan Ann is twice as sharp as you, and she’s only four years old. Sometimes you look completely soft in the head.”

Mary had scowled crossly for an hour after that, but it made her think about several entirely new things.

This morning, she stood at the window for about ten minutes after Martha had swept the hearth one last time and gone downstairs. She was thinking about the new idea that had come to her when she heard about the library. She didn't care much about the library itself, since she had read very few books, but hearing about it brought back the thought of those hundred rooms with closed doors. She wondered if they were all really locked, and what she would find if she could get into any of them. Were there really a hundred rooms? Why shouldn't she go and see how many doors she could count? It would give her something to do on a morning when she couldn't go outside. She had never been taught to ask permission to do things, and she knew nothing about rules or authority, so it wouldn't have occurred to her to ask Mrs. Medlock if she could walk around the house, even if she had run into her.

She opened the door and stepped out into the corridor, and so her wanderings began. It was a long corridor that branched into others, leading her up short flights of stairs that connected to even more passages. There were doors everywhere, and pictures hung on the walls. Sometimes they were dark, strange landscapes, but most of them were portraits of men and women in grand, old-fashioned costumes made of satin and velvet. She found herself in a long gallery where the walls were covered with these portraits. She had never imagined there could be so many pictures in a single house. As she walked slowly down the gallery, she stared at the faces, and they seemed to stare right back at her. She felt as if they were wondering what a little girl from India was doing in their home. Some of the pictures were of children—little girls in stiff satin dresses that reached the floor and flared out around them, and boys with puffed sleeves, lace collars, and long hair, or with large ruffles around their necks. She stopped to look at every child, wondering what their names were, where they had gone, and why they wore such strange clothes. One portrait showed a stiff, plain-looking little girl who looked rather like Mary herself. She wore a green brocade dress and held a green parrot on her finger. Her eyes had a sharp, curious expression.
“Where do you live now?”
Mary said aloud to her.
“I wish you were here.”

Surely no other little girl had ever spent such a strange morning. It felt as if there was no one in the entire, sprawling house but her own small self. She wandered upstairs and downstairs, through narrow passages and wide halls, where it seemed like no one else had ever walked. Since the house had so many rooms, people must have lived in them once, but now it all felt so empty that she could hardly believe anyone ever had.

It wasn't until she climbed to the second floor that she thought about trying a doorknob. All the doors were shut, just as Mrs. Medlock had said. But finally, she placed her hand on one of the handles and turned it. She felt a brief flutter of fear when the knob turned easily. When she pushed, the heavy door swung open slowly. It was a massive door, leading into a large bedroom. Embroidered tapestries hung on the walls, and the room was filled with the kind of decorated, inlaid furniture she had seen in India. A wide window with leaded glass panes looked out onto the moor, and over the fireplace hung another portrait of the stiff, plain little girl, who seemed to stare at her more curiously than ever.
“Perhaps she slept here once,”
Mary said.
“She stares at me so much, she makes me feel strange.”

After that, she opened door after door. She saw so many rooms that she began to tire, starting to believe there really were a hundred of them, even though she hadn't counted. In every room, there were old paintings or tapestries showing strange scenes. Almost all of them contained unique furniture and curious ornaments.

One room, which looked like a lady’s sitting room, had walls draped in embroidered velvet. Inside a cabinet stood about a hundred little elephants carved from ivory. They were all different sizes; some carried riders or covered carriage seats on their backs. A few were quite large, while others were so tiny they looked like babies. Having seen carved ivory in India, Mary knew all about elephants. She opened the cabinet door, stood on a footstool, and played with them for a long time. When she grew tired, she arranged them neatly and closed the cabinet door.

In all her wanderings through the long corridors and empty rooms, she had seen nothing alive—until she entered this room. Just after she closed the cabinet door, she heard a tiny rustling sound. It made her jump. She looked around at the sofa near the fireplace, where the sound seemed to come from. In the corner of the sofa lay a cushion. There was a hole in its velvet cover, and out of the hole peeped a tiny head with a pair of frightened eyes.

Mary crept softly across the room to take a closer look. The bright eyes belonged to a little gray mouse. She had chewed a hole into the cushion and made a cozy nest inside. Six baby mice were cuddled up asleep next to her. Even if there was no one else alive in those hundred rooms, these seven mice didn't look lonely at all.
“If they wouldn’t be so scared, I would take them back with me,”

Mary said.

She had wandered around long enough to feel too tired to go any further, so she turned back. She lost her way two or three times by turning down the wrong corridors, forcing her to wander up and down until she found the right path. Finally, she made it back to her own floor, though she was still some distance from her room and didn't know exactly where she was.
“I think I've made a wrong turn again,”
she said, standing still at the end of a short passage with tapestries on the wall.
“I don’t know which way to go. How quiet everything is!”

As she stood there, just after she spoke, the silence was broken by a sound. It was another cry, though not quite like the one she had heard the night before. This was short—a fretful, childish whine, muffled by the thick walls.
“It’s closer than it was,”
Mary said, her heart beating a little faster.
“And someone really is crying.”

She accidentally placed her hand on the tapestry near her, then jumped back in surprise. The tapestry was actually covering a door, which swung open to reveal another section of the corridor. Walking toward her was Mrs. Medlock, a bunch of keys in her hand and a very angry look on her face.
“What are you doing here?”
Mrs. Medlock demanded, grabbing Mary's arm and pulling her away.
“What did I tell you?”
“I took a wrong turn,”
Mary explained.
“I didn’t know which way to go, and I heard someone crying.”
She absolutely detested Mrs. Medlock at that moment, and she hated her even more a second later.
“You didn’t hear anything of the sort!”
the housekeeper snapped.
“Get back to your own nursery, or I'll box your ears.”
She grabbed Mary by the arm and half-pushed, half-pulled her up one passage and down another until she shoved her through the door of her own room.
“Now,”
Mrs. Medlock said,

“you stay where you're told, or you'll find yourself locked in. The master had better get you a governess, just like he said he would. You're someone who needs a close eye kept on her, and I've got enough to do already.”
She marched out of the room and slammed the door behind her. Mary sat down on the hearth rug, pale with rage. She didn't cry, but she ground her teeth in anger.
“There was someone crying—there was—there was!”

she whispered to herself.

She had heard it twice now, and sooner or later, she would find out the truth. She had discovered a great deal this morning. She felt as if she had been on a long journey, and at least she had found things to keep her entertained. She had played with the ivory elephants, and she had seen the gray mouse and her babies cozy in their velvet cushion nest.
